headline: High risk of prompt/data leakage and cascading errors from shared filesystem plus broad shell/network access; compliance risk is moderate.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Continue can use MCP and shares state via filesystem, while the course agent reads/writes workspace files and runs shell commands. That creates a plausible content-to-instruction bridge if one agent consumes the other's files or outputs. The pathway is documented in both profiles, though not directly observed.
conditions: IF either agent reads the other's generated files as instructions without provenance checks
IF a shared workspace or mounted directory is used by both agents
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent
Disable MCP for the Continue instance when processing untrusted content
Add a provenance prefix to files exchanged between agents
Require manual review before either agent executes instructions from files
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and instruction/data separation

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents can read and write filesystem content, and both touch sensitive classes: Continue handles open editor buffers and API keys, while the course agent handles configuration secrets and academic data. Shared storage would let either agent expose the other's sensitive material through outputs or logs. The interaction is inferred from documented capabilities, not directly evidenced.
conditions: IF both agents mount the same workspace or secrets directory
IF either agent logs or echoes file contents into its outputs
mitigations: Store secrets outside shared folders
Use separate OS users or containers
Redact secrets before passing files between agents
Turn off automatic file summarization for sensitive paths
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent access controls and audit logging

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have unrestricted filesystem write and shell execution, and Continue explicitly shares state via filesystem. Even though neither profile claims git writes, concurrent edits to the same directory can overwrite files or corrupt generated artifacts by default. Uncertainty about orchestration locking pushes this to high rather than medium.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same directory without file locks
IF either agent writes generated artifacts while the other is editing
mitigations: Assign disjoint output directories
Run only one writer at a time
Use file locks around shared artifacts
Snapshot the workspace before concurrent runs
requires-engineering: add transactional workspace coordination

D_cascading_error.rationale: Continue can produce code or file edits from chat plus MCP-driven tool use, and the course agent can act on notebooks, APIs, and shell commands. If B treats A's output as authoritative, mistakes can propagate into executed notebooks or deployed course artifacts. The pairwise pathway is plausible but not directly documented, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF B consumes A's generated text or code without verification
IF A's output is copied into notebooks or shell commands
mitigations: Require a human approval step before execution
Add automated lint/tests for generated code
Mark A outputs as drafts only
Use a checklist to verify citations and commands
requires-engineering: add schema validation between agents

E_compliance.rationale: Continue handles model provider API keys and broad network egress, while the course agent handles configuration secrets and uses allowlisted egress plus Docker/Airflow credentials. If the same regulated or secret-bearing data is processed by both, differing retention and residency assumptions can create a compliance mismatch. Only one agent needs citation because the issue is the pair's combined handling of secrets.
conditions: IF regulated secrets or personal data are shared across both agents
IF one agent's logs are retained longer than the other's
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of both agents
Rotate exposed API keys after use
Disable verbose logging
Document retention for each workspace
requires-engineering: align residency and retention controls across both systems
